analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers and Medicare to cover out-of-network routine care for clinical trial patients at in-network rates.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had bipartisan sponsorship, never received a hearing, a vote, or any action in either committee and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change insurance rules so that people enrolled in approved clinical trials can use doctors and hospitals outside their insurer's network for their routine care — doctor visits, scans, lab work — and pay only what they would pay for in-network care. It applies to private individual and employer plans and to Medicare, and it adds consultation and referral services to the list of trial-related costs that must be covered. It also lets the Health and Human Services Department explore a voluntary shared network of providers to make trial coverage easier for plans to arrange.
analysis.who_benefits: Cancer patients and other seriously ill people who join approved clinical trials but live far from, or cannot get into, the trial site's insurance network. Instead of facing out-of-network charges for routine care connected to the trial, they would owe only their normal in-network copay or coinsurance, with the insurer paying the provider the balance. This lowers a real financial barrier to trial participation and to the experimental treatments those trials test.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Clinical trial patients far from network care

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans and insurers to apply in-network cost-sharing to routine patient costs furnished by a nonparticipating (out-of-network) provider during an approved clinical trial, and to pay the provider the difference between the recognized amount and the patient's cost-sharing.

Extends the same protection to Medicare, requiring the Secretary of Health and Human Services to define routine costs of care to include consultation and referral services for participants in category A clinical trials.
Adds consultation and referral services to covered routine patient costs in private plans and adds Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute trials to the list of approved clinical trials.

Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to survey plans and insurers about interest in a voluntary network of participating providers, administered by a third-party administrator, for meeting clinical trial coverage requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and self-insured employers would pay more when trial patients use out-of-network providers at in-network rates, a cost typically passed through to premiums. The Medicare provision adds covered services, borne by the Medicare program and its financing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and the Medicare program

drawbacks.text: Plans must pay out-of-network providers at in-network cost-sharing rates even where they have no contract with that provider, which removes a tool insurers use to steer care and would add claims costs, some portion of which shows up in premiums for everyone.

The Medicare provision adds consultation and referral services to covered routine trial costs, a new obligation for the Medicare program that begins with items and services furnished on or after January 1, 2024.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is targeted but real: patients considering clinical trials often hesitate because their insurer will not cover routine care delivered at a trial site outside their network, and this bill directly removes that barrier at in-network cost-sharing. The cost is a modest expansion of insurer and Medicare payment obligations, concentrated on a small population rather than spread across all care. The bill is narrow and does not address other barriers to trial access, but nothing in it is badly designed; its main flaw is that it never moved at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jackie Speier introduced the bill on July 27, 2022, joined by Rep. Michael McCaul, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee.
The bill drew two additional cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat, in addition to the original bipartisan pair.
The action history shows no activity after the referrals to committee: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers are better off, since they avoid a new requirement to cover out-of-network routine care for trial participants at in-network rates. Patients hoping to join clinical trials at distant sites keep facing out-of-network bills for their routine care.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers that avoid new coverage duties

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship from the start — a Democrat and a Republican introduced it together, and its two later cosponsors split one to one — but it never advanced far enough for a vote that would show how the parties lined up.

industries.note: Plans would have to cover routine care from out-of-network providers during approved clinical trials at in-network cost-sharing and pay providers the balance, taking away a way insurers currently limit which doctors trial patients can use. The avoided cost is exactly the out-of-pocket burden the bill lifts from patients.
Employer group health plans are covered by the mandate, so employers would absorb somewhat higher claims costs for the small number of employees in trials at out-of-network sites.

industries.industry: Clinical trial sponsors and research networks
industries.note: Easier coverage of routine care lowers a participation barrier, which helps trials recruit patients, including for Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute trials the bill adds to the approved list.
